The study identifies inosine as a metabolite associated with improved overall survival in renal cell carcinoma (RCC) patients treated with nivolumab (ICI), based on re-analysis of the CheckMate 025 trial data.

The study reports that higher baseline plasma levels of inosine were associated with longer median overall survival (33 months vs. 22 months) in ICB-treated RCC patients, but this association was not observed in patients treated with everolimus.

The study demonstrates that inosine enhances tumor immunogenicity and sensitizes tumor cells to T-cell mediated killing by directly binding to and inhibiting the ubiquitin-activating enzyme UBA6 in tumor cells.
The study shows that UBA6 expression in human tumor tissues negatively correlates with ICB response and predicts progression-free survival in melanoma cohorts.

The study is a narrative review summarizing the role of gut microbial metabolites in cancer immunotherapy. It reports clinical observations where fecal Short-Chain Fatty Acids (SCFAs) concentrations were measured in cohorts of patients receiving PD-1 inhibitors (Nivolumab/Pembrolizumab). Specifically, it cites a cohort of 52 solid tumor patients and an NSCLC cohort of 11 patients, noting that higher fecal SCFA levels (acetate, propionate, butyrate, valerate) were associated with longer progression-free survival and beneficial effects. It also references a study on metastatic melanoma patients treated with anti-CTLA-4, where serum butyrate and propionate were inversely correlated with PFS/OS. The review details mechanisms for SCFAs, Inosine, TMAO, and Tryptophan metabolites, highlighting their potential as predictive biomarkers.

The study is a review summarizing the role of inosine in colorectal cancer (CRC) and gut homeostasis. It explicitly states that 'studies reporting the effects of the spatial redistribution of inosine across different intestinal compartments along CRC onset are currently missing since most of the clinical and preclinical data were generated from a bulk metabolomic analysis' and that 'no human studies have longitudinally tracked inosine levels'. The only clinical trial mentioned is a phase-2 study in mixed advanced solid tumors where CRC-specific results were not reported separately. The paper highlights that inosine-producing bacteria (e.g., Bifidobacterium pseudolongum) enhance ICI efficacy in preclinical mouse models via A2A receptor-mediated T cell activation, but these findings are not derived from human tumor tissue metabolite quantification.
